newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China Grain - China holds off on soybean imports.
newsitem.headline: China Grain - China holds off on soybean imports.

text.p: Fears that China's new soybean crop due in November will soften domestic prices and anticipation of a further drop in Chicago bean futures has held Chinese buyers back despite attractive price levels, traders in Hong Kong and China said on Thursday.

Grain traders said their phones were ringing off the hook as Chinese buyers called to make enquiries, but no specific deals had been concluded even as Chicago soybean futures dropped for the third consecutive day.
"The big fear is that China's new soybean crop will dampen domestic prices," said one grains trader.
If domestic prices dropped, Dalian Commodity Exchange futures would drop too and this would hamper anyone importing soybeans for delivery against futures contracts, he noted.
Chinese traders profit by importing cheaper goods on the international market and selling them at the normally higher price within China.

A 50,000-tonne cargo of U.S.-origin soybeans was heard being negotiated in Shanghai for November delivery, but fear of the new crop pushing domestic prices down has slowed talks on the contract, a Shanghai-based source said by telephone.
One Chinese enquiry for 20,000 tonnes of U.S. soybeans was heard on Thursday as China-based traders came back to work from the October 1-2 National Day holiday.
"The prices are workable for China, but the quantity is a problem for us," the grain source said.

U.S-origin cargoes came in 50,000-tonne Panamax sizes, the grain trader said, noting that he would have to find other Chinese buyers to make up a combination cargo for the trip to China from the United States.
Some of the firm's Chinese clients could not garner enough cash for a Panamax size cargo and had therefore opted for smaller lots of 20,000 tonnes.

Other grain traders noted that Chinese buyers were requesting prompt cargoes which was not always possible for sellers. "Any position beyond end-November becomes risky because of the new crop," one source said.
Offers of soybeans were heard at about $325-330 c and f Ningbo, a port in southern China. No firm Chinese bids were reported.
Deals concluded for delivery by December and January would also overlap with the beginning of Chinese New Year preparations, traders said.

Although the official dates for China's biggest holiday fall in the second week of February 1997, many migrant port workers leave much earlier to avoid snares in China's national rail network, they said.
"This could interfere with port facilities and cause demurrage," one grains trader said.
Diminished concerns about severe damage to the U.S. soybean crop drove CBOT soybean futures down on Wednesday, with November ending at $7.42 per bushel.

Traders in Hong Kong and China continued to shrug off the possiblity of Chinese corn exports, noting exports at this stage were simply not profitable, regardless of government approvals, since domestic prices were higher than international prices.
"China now operates according to the market regardless of policy," said a Chinese trader.
China denied on Wednesday that a December 1994 ban on corn exports had been lifted.
--Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843 6358
